title: Working in a Big Corp Without Feeling Like a Cog
summary: Big companies feel slow for real reasons: blast radius, coordination cost and systems that outlive teams. How to align, ship through the gates and grow on the ladder.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Say you've just moved from a 20-person startup to a company with a few thousand engineers. In week one you spot a timeout in a shared service that's clearly set too low. At your old job you'd have fixed it before lunch. Here, the service belongs to another team, the change needs their review, config only goes out in a release window, and someone asks whether you've checked with the teams that call it. It's Thursday and you haven't merged a thing.

It's easy to call that bureaucracy. Most of the time it's the price of a system that serves millions of people and has to keep working while hundreds of engineers change it every day. Once you see why the machine is built this way, you can get a lot done inside it, and have a good time doing it. This post covers where your work comes from, why so much of the senior job is writing and agreeing, how to get changes through the gates, and how people grow here.

It's the first deep-dive after the overview of big corp, startup and outsourcing, so this one goes all the way into the big-company side.

Why everything takes longer here

Size changes how the work behaves. Three things shift at once.

  • Blast radius. One bug can hit millions of users, another team's service, revenue or a compliance promise. "Move fast and break things" stops being a motto and turns into an incident review.
  • Coordination. Every new person adds a line to everyone already there. Ten people make 45 possible pairs. A hundred people make 4,950. Fred Brooks put it bluntly in The Mythical Man-Month: adding people to a late software project makes it later, partly because the talking grows faster than the team. At a big company, typing the change is the cheap part. Making it fit everyone else's changes is the expensive part.
  • Lifespan. People move on after a few years. Systems often stay for ten. Decisions have to make sense to engineers who haven't joined yet, which is why so much gets written down.

One more idea is worth knowing on day one. In 1968 Mel Conway wrote that any organization that designs a system "will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure" (Conway's law). The team boundaries you keep bumping into are usually seams in the architecture too. When a change feels hard because it crosses three teams, it's probably crossing three services as well.

Where your ticket comes from

At a startup you can often see the whole board. At a big company you see your part of it, and the board is huge. Work usually comes down through layers like these:

LayerWhat lives thereWho owns it
Company strategyMulti-year bets and themesExecutives
Org goals (OKRs)What the org wants to move this quarter or year, with a number attachedDirectors and VPs
Roadmap and epicsInitiatives cut into pieces a team can deliverProduct and engineering leads
Stories and tasksThe work you actually pick upYour team

By the time a ticket reaches you, the reason for it lives a few layers up. That's the deal at a big company: the direction is clear, and the user feels far away. Nobody asks you to guess whether your work matters, yet it's easy to lose track of how it matters. One habit helps a lot. Once a quarter, read your org's OKRs and ask which one your epic serves. When you can trace a ticket to a real user outcome, review comments make more sense, trade-offs get easier to call, and the backlog stops feeling like a queue someone handed you.

Writing is how you get agreement

Nobody mentions this before your first big-company job: a lot of senior engineering work happens before the code. You get several teams to agree on an approach before anyone builds it. With that many people involved, it's usually the fastest route. The alternative is three teams building three versions and spending a quarter merging them.

That agreement mostly runs on documents, because a doc can reach fifty readers and a meeting can't. Malte Ubl's write-up of design docs at Google is a good model. A design doc's main job is to catch design problems early, "when making changes is still cheap", and to record the trade-offs you made. He puts the sweet spot for larger projects at around 10 to 20 pages, with a 1 to 3 page "mini design doc" for smaller changes. He's also clear about when to skip it: if the problem isn't ambiguous and the doc would only say "this is how we'll implement it", write the code instead.

What goes in a design doc

Context and scope. Goals, plus non-goals (things you're choosing not to do). The design itself, at the level of diagrams, APIs and data. Alternatives you considered and why you dropped them. Cross-cutting concerns such as security, privacy and observability. People comment async, you reply, and the decision stays on record for whoever touches this system next year.

The same habit shows up in code review, where a clear PR description does a small version of the same job. More on that in How to Write a Great Pull Request. At a big company, how well you write decides how far your ideas travel.

Process: find out why the gate is there

The gates that slow you down usually exist because something expensive happened once. A security review often shows up after a data leak. A change-approval step often shows up after a Friday deploy took down checkout. A separate QA stage often shows up after a regression reached customers who couldn't live with it.

Some process has outlived its reason, though. It got copied from a place where it made sense and now mostly produces status reports. G.K. Chesterton has a well-known parable for this: before you tear down a fence, find out why someone put it up (Chesterton's fence). At work, that gives you a simple way to sort gates:

  • A gate that guards against a real, costly failure: respect it and learn its logic so you can get through it fast. Reviewers say yes sooner to people who've already answered their usual questions.
  • A gate nobody can explain: question it politely, with data, through the person who owns it. People who push for change this way get listened to. People who only grumble rarely do.
Don't fight every gate in month one

New joiners often try to tear down process in their first few weeks. Hold off. Ask the owner of each gate why it exists. Some of them carry weight you can't see from your desk. Earn the context first, then push for the change.

Deep, narrow and dependent on other teams

At a big company you usually own one piece, such as a service, a subsystem or a domain, and you go deep on it. Everything outside that piece belongs to someone else: SREs run production, DBAs look after data, a platform team owns infrastructure, a design-system team owns UI components, security signs off, and a release team owns the path to production.

That split works well, and it means a big part of your effectiveness comes from working across team lines. Know who owns what. Build the relationship before you need a favor. Write tickets another team can act on without a meeting. Respect their queue: a team that plans in two-week sprints can't do much with "I need this today", while the same request with two weeks' notice usually lands fine. If you came from a startup where you ran the database migration yourself, this is the biggest adjustment. Handing work off well is a real skill, and a hard one.

How to actually ship here

Shipping at a big company depends less on how fast you code and more on how well you find your way. A few habits work almost everywhere:

  • Find the people who really decide. The org chart gives you titles. The work shows you who actually unblocks things. Bring them in before you build, while their input is still cheap to use.
  • Write the doc first. A one-page proposal surfaces objections early and leaves a record you can point to later.
  • Keep changes small and easy to undo. Feature flags, staged rollouts and backward-compatible steps get approved faster because they're less risky to approve. Google's SRE workbook shows the math for canary releases: if a bad build fails 20% of requests but only 5% of traffic reaches it, the overall error rate is 1% instead of 20% (Canarying Releases).
  • Talk to reviewers before the review. Walk the key people through your plan one by one. The review meeting should confirm an agreement. It shouldn't be where people hear your idea for the first time.
  • Give dependencies lead time. Ask early, say when you need it and why, and check in before the date.

On Zalo PC, the habit I lean on most is the third one: risky changes ship turned off, behind a kill switch or remote config. When we rolled out PC message backup with restore on mobile, that's what let us open it up in waves and check the numbers before each step wider.

Stakeholders, and the good kind of politics

"Politics" has a bad name, and in a big org you can't avoid it. The healthy version is simple: understand what different people care about and show how your plan helps them. Your work touches a PM's roadmap, another team's on-call load and a director's OKR. When your proposal names those interests and answers them, approvals and headcount come a lot easier.

The toxic version exists too: taking credit, hoarding information, undermining peers behind their backs. Name it so you never practice it, and so you spot it when it's aimed at you. Done with integrity, stakeholder management is teamwork at a bigger size.

How big companies wear people down

Large organizations have their own ways of grinding people down. Spotting them early is half the fix.

PatternWhat it looks likeWhat helps
Nobody owns the gap"Someone else will handle it." A problem sits between two teams for months.Claim a clear scope and own its edges. Volunteer for the seams.
Meeting overloadA full calendar and no time to buildBlock focus time, shorten or decline low-value meetings, default to async updates
"Nothing changes here"People stop trying to fix thingsPick one small fixable thing and fix it. Momentum builds on itself.
Slow feedbackMonths between your work and any visible resultFind early signals, instrument your features, talk to the teams downstream
A shrinking worldDeep skill in a tiny corner and little context beyond itRotate scope on purpose, learn the systems next to yours, meet users when you can

Growing on the ladder

Of the three worlds, big companies tend to have the clearest career ladders: defined levels, written expectations and promotion reviews where a committee looks at your case alongside your manager. The rules are readable, which is a real gift. To climb them:

  • Grow your scope, not your hours. Promotions track the size of the problems you own: your task, then your team's work, then work across teams.
  • Make the impact visible. In a big org, work nobody hears about might as well not exist. Write the doc, give the demo, share the win and the credit.
  • Keep an eye on your glue work. Tanya Reilly uses glue work for the unglamorous work that keeps a team moving: unblocking people, reviewing designs, onboarding newcomers. She calls it technical leadership, and warns that doing it too early in a career, without recognition, can be "career limiting". Her advice: keep the artifacts, ask your manager directly whether this work counts toward promotion, and keep building your core technical skills.
  • Find a sponsor as well as a mentor. A mentor gives you advice. A sponsor speaks up for you in the room where promotions get decided.

If you try all of this and the pace still feels too slow, or the user still feels too far away, that's useful to know about yourself. A startup or the variety of outsourcing might suit you better right now. You can always come back.

Try this week

  • Find the OKR your current epic serves and add one line to the ticket that connects the two.
  • Before your next non-trivial change, write a one-page doc: problem, approach, alternatives, who's affected.
  • Pick one gate that slows you down and ask its owner why it exists.
  • Ship your next risky change behind a flag that's off by default.
  • Write down one piece of glue work you did this month and bring it to your next 1:1.

faqs.q: Why does everything feel so slow in a big company?
faqs.a: Mistakes are expensive and coordination is even more so. A bug can reach millions of users and other teams' services, and every change has to fit what dozens of other teams are doing. Reviews, security sign-off and change approval exist to limit that blast radius. You move faster by writing a short proposal early, keeping changes small and easy to undo, and walking reviewers through your plan before the review meeting.

Some of it is. A lot of it guards against a failure that already happened once, such as a leak or an outage. Before you try to remove a gate, ask the person who owns it why it exists. Learn the logic of the ones that protect something real so you can pass them quickly, and question the ones nobody can explain, politely and with data.

faqs.q: How do I avoid feeling like a cog in a big company?
faqs.a: Trace your work back to a goal. Read your org's OKRs and find the one your epic serves, so each ticket connects to a real user outcome. Claim a clear scope and own its edges, learn the systems next to yours, and share your work through docs and demos so people see what it changed.

faqs.q: What gets you promoted in a big company?
faqs.a: Growing the scope of the problems you own and making that growth visible: from your own tasks, to your team's work, to work across teams. Cross-team delivery, clear design docs and lower risk all count. Keep a record of your glue work and ask your manager directly whether it counts toward promotion. A sponsor who speaks up for you in promotion discussions helps a lot.

faqs.q: I came from a startup and keep getting blocked by other teams. What am I doing wrong?
faqs.a: Work that you used to do yourself, like a database migration or an infrastructure change, now belongs to specialist teams. Work through them: learn who owns what, give them lead time (a team that plans in sprints can't act on 'I need this today'), write tickets they can act on without a meeting, and build relationships before you need a favor.
